en: Turn back toward Kanykey;
If you heed my words, forty companions,
Let us go to our sister-in-law.
Though she is a woman, let us
Take our sister-in-law as our support;
Until Semetey reaches twelve,
Let us somehow rear the orphan.
When the boy reaches twelve,
Let us gird our loins firmly;
Taking the orphan as our hope,
From the Chinese in Beijing
Let us exact vengeance for our hero!
For renowned Manas, the gray-maned wolf,
Let us honor his spirit in this way;
Let us not plunder his palace.
Companions, think over my words:
For Manas, gone to the other world,
If what is told is true,
Let us not become black donkeys.
Manas's salt was precious—
How could we have forgotten his salt!
Manas's spirit was exalted—
How can we forsake his spirit?
The hoof left behind by the noble steed,
The little one, our lasting treasure,
A child still in the nursing cradle—
How can we begin violence against him?!
Is there a mountain advancing upon us?
It seems we have all girded ourselves for battle.
Forty companions, is there an enemy from Beijing?
You have readied yourselves and taken up spears;
Against an orphan and a widow
You have set out on the march.
Is there a ravine with a high bank?
With Khan Kongurbai at their head,
Is there an enemy coming from Khangai?”
The gold we gathered turned to stone;
Six scoundrels became the people's rulers.
On one side, his grandfather, Khan Zhakyp,
That swine, became his enemy.
What he dug was a deep pit;
Upon your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
A heavy misfortune fell.
An iron net fell about her feet.
After your generous Manas died,
Six scoundrels became the people's oppressors.
The forty companions would not heed him;
Poor Yrchyuul was humiliated.
Abyke, Kobosh, the six scoundrels,
Plundered the fine cloth
And wrought thorough havoc.
The scoundrels broke into the treasury;
Whole beaver pelts
They cut in halves,
And staked them in their knucklebone game.
Strutting like a slave whose master has died,
His nose bulging like a wineskin,
At that time Kobosh, over the people,
Had become the sultan.
The forty were dogs from forty different places;
All forty obeyed Kobosh's word.
Their swords swayed;
Their spears wobbled then.
Their squad leaders bobbed along;
Their spears stuck out.
There were pale, mottled banners,
And a clamor of “Boi, boi!”
There were banners with golden crescents,
And a clamor of battle cries.
The six scoundrels ruled the people
And made enemies of Kanykey.
The blue-mottled sun was eclipsed in heaven;
Yrchyuul, son of Yraman,
To his father's city
Fled openly and escaped.
A vast host came pouring on;
The boy upon her back was young—
Now misfortune would boil over!
Were I to speak to Allah, my words would be a lament.
Six months' worth of suffering
Ready to tell it at once,
Beside Kanykey
There was a naked little child.
The child upon her shoulder
Stirred and tugged at her earlobe;
Into your sister-in-law's ear
He whispered the news.
The beauty among the dark-complexioned,
The radiant one among Muslims,
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey—
Allah's sun grew overcast in heaven;
Sixty troubles came upon her at once.
For six calves and four yearlings
She had bought Ak-Tinte;
She grasped it firmly by its hilt
And entrusted it to her trusty hand.
The sixty women mourning,
Akylai seated beside the mourning effigy,
Manas's senior wife,
And the sixty women mourning—
“If only I could seize and slaughter them all!”
That was the thought your sister-in-law reached.
Seen today, gone tomorrow—
Unable to collect herself,
Kanykey stood weeping.
So that is what this shitty world is like!
“White-marked horses graze upon the hills;
If I slaughter the woman now—
Damn it, this shitty world!
The boy upon my back is young!”
Kanykey, built like a warrior,
Grew pale, her color changing;
Blood drained from her face and she trembled.
When your sister-in-law went in,
The sixty women mourning,
With Akylai at their head,
Rushed out trembling.
When your formidable sister-in-law Kanykey
Went up to Akylai,
Blue flame hissed from her mouth;
Her great teeth, broad as doors,
Shattered like millet.
Blue flame mixed with fire
Billowed from her mouth.
“Woman, from the Six Cities, from Kokand,
He became governor and took you;
From Bukhara with its unopening gates,
He took me after six raids.
You were called the honored senior wife;
It was you who sat beside the mourning effigy.
For the falcon laid out in death,
I was only the quiet junior wife.
To your father Khan Shooruk's city,
Bringing gold and golden ornaments,
Gathering goods on six bay horses,
Fighting without rest for six months,
Making six khans' peoples suffer,
Driving livestock and giving gold,
It was you he won through hardship.
From my father Khan Temir's city,
Taken by my unruly hero,
I was the wretch carried behind his saddle.
Woman, you have no shame at all!
Forty days have not yet passed since my slayer of foes died;
Your heart has turned corrupt, seeking support;
Forgetting my hero,
You seek a place well known to all.
Since the hero closed his eyes,
Woman, you have become
One who seeks a man well known to all.
Leave this palace, woman;
Reach your desire, woman.
Go to the support on whom you rely;
Go out of my sight, woman,
To that husband you mean to marry!
You too have a dwelling like mine,
You have livestock equal to mine,
You have a life like mine.
To the support on whom you rely,
Go out now, unhappy woman,
To that husband you mean to marry!”
The sixty women mourning,
With Akylai at their head,
She drove out of the palace.
Akylai rushed out trembling.
When they saw your sister-in-law's face,
The sixty women mourning
Scurried away from the palace.
“Now that the hero has closed his eyes,
How shall I attain my hope?” she said.
That heroic sister-in-law Kanykey,
Your hero's great telescope—
“I shall take it as a keepsake,” she said.
She tied it tightly once again,
Your hero's great telescope,
Into the fold of her wraparound skirt,
Fastening and securing it firmly.
“I shall keep smelling it as a keepsake,” she said.
She tied it tightly once again
Into the fold of her wraparound skirt,
Fastened it firmly and stowed it away.
Then Kanykey, the woman in mourning,
Was sorely troubled in her heart;
Then tears poured from her eyes.
Wailing, weeping, beating herself,
To her mother, the honored elder woman,
Chyiyrdy, she pleaded:
“Ah, my dear mother,
We camped beside the river, ah!
Parted from my precious one,
Mother, we are like a fire put out!
Mother, an iron net has fallen about our feet;
Mother, heavy misfortune has met our brow!
From the dark ridge and ravine
The time has come to turn away.
From the child left by the khan and prince,
Mother, the time has come to part!
Your hoof left behind by the noble steed,
Your lamp left by your son, the splendid warhorse!
Mother, your soft little gray hawk,
If he lives safely and grows up,
Your pale, mottled falcon, your morning star!
Your hoof left behind by the noble steed,
Your little one left by your son, the splendid warhorse,
Your pennant fastened to a spear,
Your gift left by your generous son!
My dear mother, ah,
They will trample upon our heads, I fear;
They will scatter the four kinds of livestock, I fear!
Your descendant left by the precious one,
Semetey, they will seize and slaughter, I fear;
The lamp left behind by the falcon,
The scoundrels will kill him, I fear.
God will strike those dogs, I think;
They will plunder the gold and live at ease, I fear!
Your lamp left behind by the falcon,
Your soft, pale-mottled female goshawk,
If he lives safely and grows up,
Your gray saker, your falcon.
Your hoof left behind by the noble steed,
From your son, the splendid warhorse,
Your little one left by the noble steed.
Your pennant fastened to a spear,
Your gift left by the generous one.
Slaughtering your only one,
Mother, they will leave us like a fire put out, I fear!
The child still in the nursing cradle—
Unless we take care and find a way,
Mother, they will wrench him from your arms, I fear!
Dragging him onto the road,
Mother, they will have the great dogs tear him, I fear!
Mother, that dear bird, the wild duck,
Flies toward the open plain without turning back.
How much must we endure,
Mother, for the child born from the womb?
That wretched bird, the harrier,
Swoops toward the open plain.
We shall perish,
Mother, for the child born from the belly.
We were a gorge; we have become a road.
Mother, parted from your khanly son,
We were princes; we have been humbled.
Mother, we were a vast lake; we have ebbed away.
Mother, when your son was alive,
We took lions from many places.
It was God's decree—
In the end, we devoured your son.
We poor souls who would not drink fermented mare's milk
Now long even for brackish water.
Mother, at the spur where the mountains end,
Mother, at the promontory of the level mountain,
On the face of broad Ak-Chiy,
At the edge of the main road,
Mother, there is your son's little enclosure;
Take shelter in that enclosure!
The camel calf left by your son,
